https://business-review.eu/tech/it/black.text: Black Friday: special offers are driving customers to the website. Can they complete their order? A button that cannot be accessed via the keyboard, a form without clear labels or an error message that is not conveyed to the screen reader can stop the user in their tracks just before they complete their order. “For us, the key change is that accessibility is starting to be viewed as a component of digital performance. A company invests in marketing to bring users to its website. The next question is whether that user can complete the action they came for on their own,” says George Onofrievici, a representative of Wawsome . The figures that show why accessibility matters for e-commerce E-commerce in Romania reached €12.9 billion in 2025, up 10% on the previous year, according to the European E-Commerce Report 2026, based on data provided by the Romanian Association of Online Shops. For 2026, the report estimates a figure of €13.5 billion. These figures include online purchases of goods and services. Read more about Visa & Raiffeisen Bank study: Who do teenagers trust on Black Friday? read more Wawsome’s analysis of accessibility needs takes into account three key figures from public statistics in Romania: • Over 974,000 people with disabilities. • Around 3.9 million people aged 65 and over. • Around 390,000 recipients of disability pensions. The categories overlap to some extent and should not be added together. These figures describe population groups relevant to the design of digital services, not the number of online shoppers or people who actually face barriers. The impact of digital barriers also extends to carers of people with disabilities and immediate family members. “For us, e-commerce is a natural starting point: when you make an online shop more accessible, you give more people the opportunity to shop and you can expand your customer base. The same applies to banks, utility providers and, in general, to companies that serve their customers online,” explains George Onofrievici . From promotional offer to payment: where an order can get stuck Digital barriers often arise at the points where the user has to choose a product, enter details or confirm an action. A promotional pop-up that cannot be closed using the keyboard, product options not recognised by a screen reader, or a form that does not explain the error can interrupt the purchasing journey. “The most common difficulty is the lack of a complete picture. Companies sometimes identify contrast issues or images without alternative text, but they do not always track the user’s entire journey. A website may have pages that look fine in an automated report, yet the user may be unable to complete the payment, may not receive a clear error message, or may be unable to navigate using the keyboard,” emphasises George Onofrievici . An increasingly important aspect of digital accessibility audits is BNPL (Buy Now, Pay Later) payment solutions, which allow shoppers to pay for products in instalments or at a later date. These methods often involve redirecting the user to the financial service provider’s platform, where they must complete additional steps for identification, authentication or approval of the financing. If forms cannot be completed using only the keyboard, if fields are not interpreted correctly by screen readers, or if error messages are not communicated in an accessible format, users may encounter difficulties or be prevented from completing the transaction. During periods of high transaction volumes, such as Black Friday, these barriers can turn a nearly completed order into a lost sale, even if the accessibility issues arise outside the merchant’s platform. Practical examples: removing bottlenecks from an online service During digital accessibility audits carried out for clients in the e-commerce sector, Wawsome’s specialists identified barriers affecting various stages of the purchasing process: product filters that could not be used exclusively with the keyboard, ‘Add to basket’ buttons that were not correctly recognised by screen readers, pop-up windows that users could not close using the keyboard, checkout forms with fields lacking accessible labels, and payment error messages that were not communicated via assistive technologies. Additional attention is also given to BNPL (Buy Now, Pay Later) payment flows, which allow purchases to be paid for in instalments or at a later date. These may involve redirecting the buyer to the financial service provider’s platform or completing additional steps within an interface integrated into the checkout process. The issues identified during client audits were documented and prioritised by Wawsome’s specialists, and the technical teams implemented the necessary fixes. Following these changes, product filters became keyboard-operable, purchase buttons could be identified by screen readers, pop-up windows no longer blocked navigation, checkout fields were given accessible labels, and error messages became perceivable to users of assistive technologies. For payment flows involving external providers, the accessibility audit covered the entire customer journey, including the authentication and payment authorisation stages, not just the online shop’s interface. Five checks to carry out before Black Friday Wawsome recommends prioritising the elements that directly affect order fulfilment: • Menus and promotional windows: these can be accessed and closed using the keyboard. • Product pages: descriptions, prices and selection options can be understood using a screen reader. • Shopping basket: changing quantities and applying discounts can be done without a mouse. • Forms: fields have clear labels, and error messages indicate what needs to be corrected. • Payment and confirmation: the entire payment process must be accessible, including when the user is redirected to third-party platforms, such as payment processors or BNPL (Buy Now, Pay Later) services. Data entry forms, identification and authentication steps, transaction authorisation and payment confirmation must be navigable using a keyboard and assistive technologies. Error messages must be accessible, and returning to the online shop must not interrupt the order completion process. Automated testing must be supplemented by manual testing of key workflows. Subsequent monitoring helps to identify issues that may arise with the introduction of promotional pages, forms or new features. Wawsome estimates the Romanian market for digital accessibility software to be worth approximately €4.1–7 million annually. This range is the company’s own extrapolation based on the global figure highlighted in the Fortune study, not a measured market value, and includes both widget- and scanner-type solutions, as well as audit, consultancy, development, remediation and training services. The Romanian Digitalisation Authority (ADR) provides information on accessibility and how to report issues at www.adr.gov.ro/accesibilitate-site-uri-web. Reports falling within the ADR’s remit can be sent to monitorizare.accesibilitateweb@adr.gov.ro. Wawsome is a European digital accessibility platform based on artificial intelligence, designed to support organisations in identifying, rectifying and monitoring digital accessibility issues, in accordance with relevant standards and regulatory frameworks, such as WCAG, EN 301 549, the European Accessibility Act (EAA) and applicable national legislation. The platform offers accessibility tools, ranging from manual auditing, monitoring and verification to automated support, as well as no-code implementation options, for organisations wishing to improve access to digital services for all users.
